summary: Defines CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE), a way to sign, authenticate and encrypt data in the compact CBOR format. It also describes how to represent cryptographic keys using CBOR. It was replaced by RFC 9052 and RFC 9053.

plainLanguage.summary: A tiny envelope-and-seal system for compact messages, so devices can sign or lock them. It has since been replaced by newer RFCs.

subtitle: Sign, encrypt, and MAC data in the compact CBOR format for IoT and constrained devices.

tldr.problem: CBOR is a compact data format designed for IoT and constrained devices, but it lacks standard ways to add signatures, encryption, and authentication codes to CBOR data.
tldr.mechanism: COSE defines six message types—COSE_Sign, COSE_Sign1 (for signing), COSE_Encrypt, COSE_Encrypt0 (for encryption), and COSE_Mac, COSE_Mac0 (for authentication codes)—each with protected and unprotected header buckets, a payload, and algorithm-specific fields. It reuses cryptographic algorithms from JOSE but optimizes them for CBOR and small message size.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now sign, authenticate, and encrypt CBOR messages with a compact encoding that fits constrained systems. RFC 9052 and RFC 9053 split and updated COSE in 2022.

today: RFC 8152 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2017. It was obsoleted in August 2022 by RFC 9052 and RFC 9053, which split signing/encryption from algorithms and made clarifications and additions to the original design. The original RFC 8152 specification is no longer normative; RFC 9052 and 9053 are the current standards.

sections.title: Security for Compact Data
sections.content:
CBOR (Concise Binary Object Representation) is a small, efficient data format inspired by JSON but designed for IoT, embedded systems, and constrained networks. The JOSE working group created JSON Web Signature (JWS) and JSON Web Encryption (JWE) for JSON data. COSE does the same for CBOR, but optimized for the different capabilities and constraints of CBOR.

COSE defines how to sign data (digitally prove who created it), encrypt data (keep it secret), authenticate it with a Message Authentication Code (MAC, verify it has not been altered), and represent cryptographic keys. All structures are built on CBOR arrays and use protected and unprotected header buckets, allowing some information to be cryptographically protected and some to be transmitted in the clear.

The RFC is a Proposed Standard that has since been obsoleted by RFC 9052 (signing and encryption) and RFC 9053 (algorithms), which clarified and extended the design.
sections.plainLanguage: COSE is a way to lock, sign, and check CBOR messages. It is like putting a seal on an envelope so you can tell if someone opened it or if it came from who you think.

sections.title: The COSE Message Structure
sections.content:
All COSE messages are CBOR arrays built from three common elements: a protected header (a binary-encoded map of cryptographically protected parameters), an unprotected header (a map of parameters that are not protected), and a payload (the message content). Elements after these three are message-type specific.

COSE defines six top-level message types. COSE_Sign and COSE_Sign1 attach one or more digital signatures to data. COSE_Sign supports multiple signers; COSE_Sign1 is simpler, for one signer. COSE_Encrypt and COSE_Encrypt0 encrypt data. COSE_Encrypt supports multiple recipients; COSE_Encrypt0 encrypts for one recipient. COSE_Mac and COSE_Mac0 compute and verify MACs (keyed authentication codes). Each message type can be identified by a CBOR tag (98, 18, 96, 16, 97, 17 respectively) or by context (e.g., a content type in HTTP).

The protected header is encoded as a byte string containing the CBOR encoding of the header map. This wrapping prevents re-encoding issues: the exact byte string is signed or authenticated, so the receiver does not need to match an encoding scheme.
sections.plainLanguage: A COSE message is a CBOR array with three parts: secret stuff, public stuff, and the message. After that, it has signatures, encrypted keys, or authentication tags depending on what you want to do.

sections.title: Signing Messages
sections.content:
COSE_Sign allows one or more signers to sign the same payload. It separates content headers (e.g., content type) from signature headers (e.g., the signing algorithm). Each signature is a COSE_Signature structure that contains its own protected and unprotected headers and the signature bytes.

COSE_Sign1 is simpler: it combines content and signature headers into one pair of buckets, so there is only one signer. To create a signature, COSE constructs a Sig_structure (a CBOR array with a context string, protected headers, external authenticated data, and the payload), encodes it to bytes, and signs those bytes.

Counter signatures are supported: a second party can sign a COSE message or signature without decrypting it, useful for timestamping or proxy signatures. Counter signatures can appear in any COSE message type, not just signed messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Sign a message by encoding the headers and payload into a byte string, signing it, and putting the signature in the message. COSE_Sign allows many signatures; COSE_Sign1 allows one.

sections.title: Encrypting Messages
sections.content:
COSE_Encrypt encrypts a payload and allows for multiple recipients. For each recipient, the content encryption key (CEK) is encrypted using one of five methods: direct (the CEK is known beforehand), key wrap (symmetric key encryption), key agreement (using public keys), key transport (asymmetric encryption), or password-based derivation.

COSE_Encrypt0 is simpler: it encrypts for a single recipient where the key is already known. There is no recipient structure; the receiver must know which key to use from context.

The encryption process creates an Enc_structure with a context string, protected headers, and external authenticated data, then encrypts the plaintext with an Authenticated Encryption with Authenticated Data (AEAD) algorithm like AES-GCM. The ciphertext and authentication tag are combined. Multiple recipients are supported by recursively encrypting the CEK for each recipient.
sections.plainLanguage: Encrypt a message by encoding headers and payload, running an encryption algorithm, and creating encrypted keys for each recipient. COSE_Encrypt supports many recipients; COSE_Encrypt0 assumes the recipient knows the key.

sections.title: Message Authentication Codes
sections.content:
COSE_Mac computes a keyed authentication code to verify the message has not been modified and optionally to verify who sent it. Like COSE_Encrypt, it supports multiple recipients and uses the same five content key distribution methods to encrypt the MAC key for each recipient.

COSE_Mac0 is simpler: it MAC's a message for a single recipient where the key is already known.

To compute a MAC, COSE constructs a MAC_structure with a context string, protected headers, external authenticated data, and the payload, encodes it, and applies the MAC algorithm (e.g., HMAC-256/64 or AES-CBC-MAC). The resulting tag is placed in the message.
sections.plainLanguage: A MAC is a checksum that uses a secret key. If the key and message are right, the checksum matches. COSE_Mac supports multiple recipients; COSE_Mac0 assumes one.

sections.title: Algorithms and Keys
sections.content:
COSE defines which cryptographic algorithms can be used. For signing, it includes ECDSA (NIST curves) and EdDSA (Edwards curves). For MACs, it includes HMAC and AES-CBC-MAC. For encryption, it includes AES-GCM, AES-CCM, and ChaCha20/Poly1305. Key derivation uses HKDF (HMAC-based extract-and-expand).

COSE represents keys as COSE_Key structures, which are CBOR maps containing key type, key parameters, and optional key identifiers. Supported key types include elliptic curve keys (for signing or key agreement), symmetric keys, and octet key pairs. Keys can carry metadata like an algorithm or a key identifier for lookup.

Algorithms are identified by integers from IANA registries, allowing compact encoding. Applications can define algorithm profiles to restrict which algorithms are allowed.
sections.plainLanguage: COSE supports popular encryption and signature algorithms like AES, ECDSA, and EdDSA. Keys are CBOR maps containing the key material and information about how to use them.
